newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China's dirtiest city in uphill battle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China's dirtiest city in uphill battle.

text.p: For years, authorities in China's far-flung western metropolis of Chongqing had difficulty making up their minds what tree should decorate the city's streets.

Chongqing authorities replaced locust trees with eucalyptus, which were in turn displaced by parasols and later banyan trees, not because the city had money to throw around or because one species was prettier than another.
Rather, they were searching for a species that would not die from constant battering by acid rain.
"More acid rain is dumped on Chongqing than any city in the world," said Xu Yu, vice-director of the Chongqing Institute of Environmental Science and Monitoring.
"There's no hiding from it," Xu said in a recent interview.
Environmental officials blame the acid rain on the use of highly sulphurous coal.
About 2,000 hectares (4,900 acres) of the Nanshan forest were destroyed in 1990 by insects that were attracted to and devoured leaves polluted by sulphur.
But neither Chongqing nor the rest of China is about to cut back on coal consumption.
WORLD'S LARGEST COAL PRODUCER, CONSUMER
China is the world's largest producer and consumer of coal -- the cheapest form of energy and the easiest to transport.
Chongqing consumed 15 million tonnes of coal in 1996 compared with about 10 million tonnes some 10 years ago, with 75 percent of the city's power generated by coal.
The metropolis emits 800,000 tonnes of sulphur dioxide each year compared with 60,000 tonnes in industrialised Hiroshima, Japan.
The pollution is taking its toll on the health of residents. The incidence of lung cancer in Chongqing is 1.7 times higher than in neighbouring cities.
Many Chongqing residents suffer respiratory problems, including asthma. One year, all examinees from Chongqing flunked tests to join the air force because of nasal problems.
HEFTY PRICE FOR ECONOMIC BOOM

Chongqing's population -- China's biggest -- doubled to 30 million in mid-March after parliament voted to elevate the city's political status to provincial-rank, a move that would aggravate the burden on municipal officials.
The city has paid a hefty price for its economic boom and fog in the winter worsens the situation.
"Pollution has worsened along with economic reforms," Acting Mayor Pu Haiqing said.
Chongqing's is one of China's top 10 steel makers, with production of 1.54 million tonnes in 1995.
It is one of China's top four automobile and motorcycle manufacturers. Motorcycle output totalled 2.19 million units in 1995, accounting for 28 percent of the national total.
The city has almost 10,000 factories employing about 1.2 million people. Industrial output was 72.9 billion yuan ($8.8 billion) in 1996.

Much of their equipment is old, making things worse. The industrialisation of Chongqing took off in the 1930s when the late Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek made it China's wartime capital, known then as Chungking.
A CITY UNFIT FOR HUMAN BEINGS
Chongqing is arguably China's dirtiest city, losing about three percent of its gross domestic product each year to pollution and ecological damage.
"Chongqing is not fit for human beings to live in," one resident surnamed Li said.
But not everyone is complaining.
"First we have to keep warm during winter and fill our stomachs," another resident said when asked if the pollution bothered him.
Thanks to air pollution, Chongqing's shoe shiners do brisk business. Some jobless people carry a can of paint and a roller as they roam Chongqing's streets looking for business.
Paint peels off buildings three times faster in Chongqing than in China's capital Beijing due to acid rain.
Shampoo sells well when it rains.
Chongqing is desperate to curb pollution and some factories have been closed.
"Old sources of pollution must be gradually cleaned up. New projects must not be a new source of pollution," Mayor Pu said.

But environmentalists say Chongqing is fighting an uphill battle against pollution, and the situation could worsen with rapid economic growth forecast since the elevation of the city's political profile.
